quests.conceptTitle: Modal Meter: Shall vs Will
quests.question: ___ we meet at the usual cafe at nine, then?
quests.targetSentence: Shall we meet at the usual cafe at nine, then?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Shall we...?' is the natural way to suggest a shared plan, especially in British English, rather than 'will', which doesn't suit suggestions this way.
quests.nativeTip: Two people are proposing and agreeing on a plan together.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎚️ Modal 'Shall' (Obligation / Certainty (100%)) ➔ 'Shall we meet at the usual cafe at nine, then?'

quests.conceptTitle: Modal Meter: Shall vs Will
quests.question: The results ___ be announced on the company website next Monday.
quests.targetSentence: The results will be announced on the company website next Monday.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Will' is the standard, neutral way to talk about the future. 'Shall' with a third-person subject like 'the results' would sound old-fashioned or overly formal here.
quests.nativeTip: This is a simple, neutral statement about a future event.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎚️ Modal 'will' (Obligation / Certainty (100%)) ➔ 'The results will be announced on the company website next Monday.'

quests.conceptTitle: Modal Meter: Shall vs Will
quests.question: ___ I open a window? It's quite stuffy in here.
quests.targetSentence: Shall I open a window? It's quite stuffy in here.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Shall I...?' is a natural, polite way to offer to do something for someone, more common than 'Will I...?' for offers.
quests.nativeTip: The speaker is offering to do something helpful.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎚️ Modal 'Shall' (Obligation / Certainty (100%)) ➔ 'Shall I open a window? It's quite stuffy in here.'

quests.conceptTitle: Modal Meter: Permission Practice: can/may
quests.question: Employees ___ park in the visitor spots after 6 p.m., according to the memo.
quests.targetSentence: Employees may park in the visitor spots after 6 p.m., according to the memo.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'May' fits the formal register of a company memo describing a specific permission, rather than a strict requirement.
quests.nativeTip: This describes an official permission stated in a company memo.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎚️ Modal 'may' (Possibility (25%)) ➔ 'Employees may park in the visitor spots after 6 p.m., according to the memo.'

quests.conceptTitle: Modal Meter: Permission Practice: can/may
quests.question: ___ I take a picture of the menu to show my friend?
quests.targetSentence: Can I take a picture of the menu to show my friend?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Can' suits this everyday, casual permission request in a restaurant setting between a customer and staff.
quests.nativeTip: A customer is casually asking a waiter for permission.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎚️ Modal 'Can' (Ability / Willingness (50%)) ➔ 'Can I take a picture of the menu to show my friend?'

quests.conceptTitle: Modal Meter: Permission Practice: can/may
quests.question: Only accredited journalists ___ enter the press conference room.
quests.targetSentence: Only accredited journalists may enter the press conference room.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'May' expresses formal permission restricted to a specific group, fitting the official tone of a press event.
quests.nativeTip: This is an official rule limiting who is allowed inside.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎚️ Modal 'may' (Possibility (25%)) ➔ 'Only accredited journalists may enter the press conference room.'

quests.conceptTitle: Modal Meter: Advice vs Preference: should vs would
quests.question: If I were you, I ___ wait until the sale starts before buying it.
quests.targetSentence: If I were you, I would wait until the sale starts before buying it.
quests.grammarRule: Advice vs Preference: should vs would
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Would' is used in the fixed hypothetical phrase 'If I were you, I would...' to give advice indirectly, through an imagined situation.
quests.nativeTip: This is imagined advice framed as 'if I were you'.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎚️ Modal 'would' (Ability / Willingness (50%)) ➔ 'If I were you, I would wait until the sale starts before buying it.'

quests.conceptTitle: Modal Meter: Advice vs Preference: should vs would
quests.question: You ___ probably back up your files before updating the system.
quests.targetSentence: You should probably back up your files before updating the system.
quests.grammarRule: Advice vs Preference: should vs would
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Should' gives direct, practical advice about a sensible precaution, without needing the hypothetical framing that 'would' requires.
quests.nativeTip: This is direct, practical advice about what is wise to do.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎚️ Modal 'should' (Advice / Expectation (75%)) ➔ 'You should probably back up your files before updating the system.'

quests.conceptTitle: Modal Meter: Advice vs Preference: should vs would
quests.question: Honestly, I ___ rather stay home tonight than go to another party.
quests.targetSentence: Honestly, I would rather stay home tonight than go to another party.
quests.grammarRule: Advice vs Preference: should vs would
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Would rather' is a fixed expression for expressing a preference, quite different from the advice-giving function of 'should'.
quests.nativeTip: This expresses a personal preference between two choices.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎚️ Modal 'would' (Ability / Willingness (50%)) ➔ 'Honestly, I would rather stay home tonight than go to another party.'

quests.conceptTitle: Modal Meter: Could vs Would
quests.question: Years ago, this shop ___ deliver groceries the same day you ordered.
quests.targetSentence: Years ago, this shop could deliver groceries the same day you ordered.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Could' expresses a general past ability - the shop was capable of same-day delivery, a fact about its former service, not a repeated ritual.
quests.nativeTip: This describes a general past ability the shop had, not a habit.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎚️ Modal 'could' (Possibility (25%)) ➔ 'Years ago, this shop could deliver groceries the same day you ordered.'

quests.conceptTitle: Modal Meter: Could vs Would
quests.question: Every Sunday, my uncle ___ take us fishing at the old pier.
quests.targetSentence: Every Sunday, my uncle would take us fishing at the old pier.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Would' fits a repeated past habit or ritual, unlike 'could', which describes a general capability rather than a recurring action.
quests.nativeTip: This describes a repeated weekly routine, not a one-time ability.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎚️ Modal 'would' (Ability / Willingness (50%)) ➔ 'Every Sunday, my uncle would take us fishing at the old pier.'

quests.conceptTitle: Modal Meter: Could vs Would
quests.question: ___ you consider rescheduling the call to Thursday instead?
quests.targetSentence: Would you consider rescheduling the call to Thursday instead?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Would you consider...?' politely invites someone to think about an option, a common professional phrasing distinct from a direct ability question.
quests.nativeTip: This is a polite way of asking someone to think about doing something.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎚️ Modal 'Would' (Ability / Willingness (50%)) ➔ 'Would you consider rescheduling the call to Thursday instead?'

quests.conceptTitle: Modal Meter: Permission Register Round 2
quests.question: Passengers ___ recline their seats once the seatbelt sign is off.
quests.targetSentence: Passengers may recline their seats once the seatbelt sign is off.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'May' matches the formal register of an official airline announcement, more appropriate than the casual 'can' in this context.
quests.nativeTip: This is an announcement in a formal, official airline tone.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎚️ Modal 'may' (Possibility (25%)) ➔ 'Passengers may recline their seats once the seatbelt sign is off.'

quests.conceptTitle: Modal Meter: Permission Register Round 2
quests.question: You ___ sit anywhere you like - we don't assign seats here.
quests.targetSentence: You can sit anywhere you like - we don't assign seats here.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Can' fits this relaxed, conversational tone between a host and a guest, where 'may' would feel unnecessarily stiff.
quests.nativeTip: A casual host is speaking informally to a guest.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎚️ Modal 'can' (Ability / Willingness (50%)) ➔ 'You can sit anywhere you like - we don't assign seats here.'

quests.conceptTitle: Modal Meter: Permission Register Round 2
quests.question: Under the new policy, remote staff ___ choose their own working hours.
quests.targetSentence: Under the new policy, remote staff may choose their own working hours.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'May' suits the formal, policy-driven tone here, describing a right granted by an official workplace rule.
quests.nativeTip: This describes an official entitlement introduced by company policy.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎚️ Modal 'may' (Possibility (25%)) ➔ 'Under the new policy, remote staff may choose their own working hours.'

quests.conceptTitle: Modal Meter: Shall vs Should
quests.question: ___ we discuss the budget first, before moving to the next item?
quests.targetSentence: Shall we discuss the budget first, before moving to the next item?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Shall we...?' proposes a joint action, whereas 'should' would instead ask whether it is advisable, a subtly different function.
quests.nativeTip: This is a suggestion proposing a shared next step.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎚️ Modal 'Shall' (Obligation / Certainty (100%)) ➔ 'Shall we discuss the budget first, before moving to the next item?'

quests.conceptTitle: Modal Meter: Shall vs Should
quests.question: You ___ double-check the numbers before submitting the report.
quests.targetSentence: You should double-check the numbers before submitting the report.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Should' gives individual advice about a wise action, unlike 'shall', which is mainly used for offers or suggestions involving 'I' or 'we'.
quests.nativeTip: This is personal advice directed at one listener.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎚️ Modal 'should' (Advice / Expectation (75%)) ➔ 'You should double-check the numbers before submitting the report.'

quests.conceptTitle: Modal Meter: Shall vs Should
quests.question: ___ I read the instructions aloud so everyone can follow along?
quests.targetSentence: Shall I read the instructions aloud so everyone can follow along?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Shall I...?' naturally offers to perform an action for others, a distinct function from the advice-based 'should'.
quests.nativeTip: The speaker is offering to do something for the group.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎚️ Modal 'Shall' (Obligation / Certainty (100%)) ➔ 'Shall I read the instructions aloud so everyone can follow along?'

quests.conceptTitle: Modal Meter: Urgency Contrast: had better vs should
quests.question: You ___ better leave for the airport now - traffic is already building up.
quests.targetSentence: You had better leave for the airport now - traffic is already building up.
quests.grammarRule: Urgency Contrast: had better vs should
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Had better' signals urgent advice with an immediate negative consequence (missing the flight), stronger than the general recommendation of 'should'.
quests.nativeTip: There's real urgency here, with a clear risk if delayed.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎚️ Modal 'had' (Modal Function (50%)) ➔ 'You had better leave for the airport now - traffic is already building up.'

quests.conceptTitle: Modal Meter: Urgency Contrast: had better vs should
quests.question: You ___ drink more water throughout the day - it's good for your health.
quests.targetSentence: You should drink more water throughout the day - it's good for your health.
quests.grammarRule: Urgency Contrast: had better vs should
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Should' fits general lifestyle advice without immediate urgency, unlike 'had better', which implies a specific, pressing situation.
quests.nativeTip: This is general, ongoing wellness advice, not an urgent warning.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎚️ Modal 'should' (Advice / Expectation (75%)) ➔ 'You should drink more water throughout the day - it's good for your health.'

quests.conceptTitle: Modal Meter: Urgency Contrast: had better vs should
quests.question: We ___ better call ahead - the restaurant gets fully booked on weekends.
quests.targetSentence: We had better call ahead - the restaurant gets fully booked on weekends.
quests.grammarRule: Urgency Contrast: had better vs should
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Had better' warns of a specific likely problem (not getting a table) if the advice isn't followed promptly.
quests.nativeTip: There's a real risk of a bad outcome if this isn't done soon.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎚️ Modal 'had' (Modal Function (50%)) ➔ 'We had better call ahead - the restaurant gets fully booked on weekends.'

quests.conceptTitle: Modal Meter: Consolidation: ought to vs should
quests.question: Landlords ___ to give proper notice before entering a tenant's home.
quests.targetSentence: Landlords ought to give proper notice before entering a tenant's home.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Ought to' is required here because 'to' follows the blank; 'should' would need to appear without 'to' to fit the same meaning.
quests.nativeTip: Check what follows the blank to decide between these two similar modals.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎚️ Modal 'ought' (Modal Function (50%)) ➔ 'Landlords ought to give proper notice before entering a tenant's home.'

quests.conceptTitle: Modal Meter: Consolidation: ought to vs should
quests.question: You really ___ apologise to your sister for what you said.
quests.targetSentence: You really should apologise to your sister for what you said.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since no 'to' follows, 'should' is the grammatically correct option, even though 'ought to' carries a very similar meaning.
quests.nativeTip: No 'to' follows the blank this time.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎚️ Modal 'should' (Advice / Expectation (75%)) ➔ 'You really should apologise to your sister for what you said.'

quests.conceptTitle: Modal Meter: Consolidation: ought to vs should
quests.question: Schools ___ to provide equal opportunities for every student.
quests.targetSentence: Schools ought to provide equal opportunities for every student.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Ought to' fits because of the following 'to', expressing what is morally the right thing for schools to do.
quests.nativeTip: Again, notice the small word that follows the blank.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎚️ Modal 'ought' (Modal Function (50%)) ➔ 'Schools ought to provide equal opportunities for every student.'

quests.conceptTitle: Modal Meter: Deduction Contrast: must vs can't
quests.question: She's answering every question instantly - she ___ know this topic extremely well.
quests.targetSentence: She's answering every question instantly - she must know this topic extremely well.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Must' draws a confident positive conclusion from clear evidence (her quick, accurate answers).
quests.nativeTip: The evidence strongly supports a positive conclusion.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎚️ Modal 'must' (Obligation / Certainty (100%)) ➔ 'She's answering every question instantly - she must know this topic extremely well.'

quests.conceptTitle: Modal Meter: Deduction Contrast: must vs can't
quests.question: He said he's never left the country, so that photo ___ have been taken abroad.
quests.targetSentence: He said he's never left the country, so that photo can't have been taken abroad.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Can't have' expresses a confident negative conclusion - the evidence makes it nearly impossible that the photo was taken abroad.
quests.nativeTip: The evidence rules out one possibility almost completely.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎚️ Modal 'can't' (Modal Function (50%)) ➔ 'He said he's never left the country, so that photo can't have been taken abroad.'

quests.conceptTitle: Modal Meter: Deduction Contrast: must vs can't
quests.question: The store is completely empty and dark - it ___ be closed today.
quests.targetSentence: The store is completely empty and dark - it must be closed today.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Must' expresses a confident positive deduction based directly on the observed evidence (empty, dark store).
quests.nativeTip: The visible evidence points strongly to one clear conclusion.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎚️ Modal 'must' (Obligation / Certainty (100%)) ➔ 'The store is completely empty and dark - it must be closed today.'

quests.conceptTitle: Modal Meter: Integrated Review: Core Contrasts
quests.question: ___ you please confirm your seat number before we begin boarding?
quests.targetSentence: Could you please confirm your seat number before we begin boarding?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Could you...?' politely requests an action in a professional airline context, more courteous than the plainer 'can'.
quests.nativeTip: Staff are speaking politely and formally to passengers.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎚️ Modal 'Could' (Possibility (25%)) ➔ 'Could you please confirm your seat number before we begin boarding?'

quests.conceptTitle: Modal Meter: Integrated Review: Core Contrasts
quests.question: You ___ update your password every ninety days, per company policy.
quests.targetSentence: You must update your password every ninety days, per company policy.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Must' expresses a required company policy, distinct from the merely advisable tone of 'should'.
quests.nativeTip: This is a mandatory security rule, not optional advice.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎚️ Modal 'must' (Obligation / Certainty (100%)) ➔ 'You must update your password every ninety days, per company policy.'

quests.conceptTitle: Modal Meter: Integrated Review: Core Contrasts
quests.question: The lights in his office are off - he ___ have gone home early.
quests.targetSentence: The lights in his office are off - he might have gone home early.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Might' expresses a tentative possibility, weaker than the confident deduction 'must' would express with stronger evidence.
quests.nativeTip: This is just one possible explanation among others.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎚️ Modal 'might' (Possibility (25%)) ➔ 'The lights in his office are off - he might have gone home early.'
